definition: A complete protocol instruction. In the MIDI 1.0 byte-stream format it has a status and the data bytes required by that message type; running status can omit a repeated channel status on the wire, and real-time bytes can interrupt other messages.
example: A Program Change is two bytes in total (Cn pp); a Note On is three (9n kk vv).

definition: A byte that carries data (values) rather than control or header information. In MIDI 1.0 specifically, a data byte has its top bit (bit 7) clear, so its value is 0x00 to 0x7F (0 to 127), and it carries values such as a note's key number and velocity.
example: In 90 3C 64, the data bytes 3C and 64 are key 60 and velocity 100.

definition: Half a byte: four bits, represented by one hexadecimal digit (0 to F). In MIDI 1.0 channel messages, the status byte’s high nibble identifies the message type and its low nibble identifies the channel; system statuses use the low nibble differently.
example: In the status byte 0x93, the high nibble 9 means Note On and the low nibble 3 means channel 4.

definition: One of sixteen addressed MIDI 1.0 parts on a connection. Channel voice and mode messages encode the selected channel in the status byte’s low nibble: zero through fifteen on the wire correspond to displayed channels one through sixteen.
example: A synth set to receive on channel 10 listens for status bytes ending in 9, such as 0x99.

definition: A MIDI receiver mode in which Channel Voice messages are accepted from all sixteen channels. Channel Mode messages still use the configured Basic Channel; Omni does not turn every channel-addressed message into a global command.
example: With omni on, a synth plays notes sent on channel 1 and channel 10 alike.

definition: Describes an instrument that can play several different sounds at once, usually each on its own MIDI channel, as if it were several instruments in one box.
example: A multitimbral synth might play a bass patch on channel 1 and a pad on channel 2 at the same time.

definition: The performance value in a MIDI 1.0 Note Off, commonly representing how fast a key was released. A transmitter without release-velocity sensing should send 64; a zero-velocity Note On is the equivalent note ending with a default release velocity.
example: 80 3C 40 is a note off with release velocity 64 (0x40).

definition: The MIDI messages that control the sound on one channel: Note On, Note Off, Poly Key Pressure, Control Change, Program Change, Channel Pressure and Pitch Bend.
example: B0 4A 50 (CC 74 = 80 on channel 1) is a channel voice message.

definition: MIDI Control Change numbers 120–127, which affect channel-wide behaviour such as silence, controller reset, Local Control and MIDI omni, monophonic or polyphonic modes. The mode changes also cause All Notes Off.
example: B0 7B 00 is All Notes Off (CC 123) on channel 1.

definition: A pair of Control Changes (CC 0 for the MSB, CC 32 for the LSB) that chooses a bank of up to 128 programs. The new bank takes effect when the following Program Change arrives.
example: B0 00 01, B0 20 00, C0 05 selects program 5 in the bank whose MSB is 1 and LSB is 0.

definition: How far a full pitch bend moves the pitch, in semitones and cents. It is Registered Parameter Number 0 and is often ±2 semitones by default.
example: With a ±12 semitone range, full upward bend raises a note by an octave.

definition: Extra pressure applied to a key after it has been pressed down, sent as MIDI pressure messages. It is often used for vibrato, volume or brightness.
example: Leaning into a held chord can add vibrato through aftertouch.

definition: A MIDI 1.0 pressure message with one data byte for the whole channel, unlike Poly Key Pressure which includes a key number. The MIDI message summary describes the greatest pressure among the depressed keys as its source value.
example: D0 50 sends a pressure of 80 on channel 1.

definition: A MIDI aftertouch message (status 0xAn) carrying a separate pressure value for each key, so each held note can be shaped individually.
example: A0 3C 40 sets the pressure on key 60 to 64.

definition: A MIDI 1.0 value assembled from two seven-bit parts, giving 16,384 possible values. Controllers zero through thirty-one have corresponding fine controllers thirty-two higher; pitch bend also has fourteen-bit resolution but uses its own message.
example: MSB 64 and LSB 32 combine to 64 × 128 + 32 = 8,224.

definition: Registered Parameter Number: a standard way to set extra parameters with Control Changes, choosing the parameter with CC 101 and 100 and then setting it with Data Entry (CC 6 and 38). RPN 0 is pitch bend sensitivity.
example: B0 65 00, B0 64 00, B0 06 0C sets a ±12 semitone bend range on channel 1.

definition: Non-Registered Parameter Number: like an RPN, but selected with CC 99 and 98 and defined by each manufacturer, so its meaning depends on the device.
example: Elektron's manuals list which NRPNs each Digitakt knob sends.

definition: Control Change 6 (coarse) and 38 (fine), used to set the value of whichever RPN or NRPN was last selected.
example: After selecting RPN 0, B0 06 0C sets the bend range to 12 semitones.

definition: Control Changes 70–79, defined for sound-shaping parameters with suggested defaults: for example 71 for timbre (often resonance), 72 release, 73 attack and 74 brightness (often filter cutoff).
example: Many synths respond to CC 74 by opening the filter.

definition: A wheel or lever beside a keyboard that sends Control Change 1, usually to add vibrato or other modulation.
example: Pushing the mod wheel up sends CC 1 values rising towards 127.

definition: A foot pedal that holds notes on after their keys are released, sent as Control Change 64: 63 or below is off, 64 or above is on. While it is down, note offs are remembered and applied when it is released.
example: B0 40 7F presses the sustain pedal on channel 1; B0 40 00 releases it.

definition: Control Change 7, which sets the overall volume of everything on one MIDI channel.
example: B0 07 64 sets channel 1's volume to 100.

definition: MIDI Channel Mode CC 123 requests release of MIDI-started notes, normally through their release envelopes. Sustain can defer release; the specification says to ignore it while Omni is on. Support is optional, so transmitters still send individual note endings.
example: B0 7B 00 sends All Notes Off on channel 1.

definition: Channel Mode message CC 120: tells a receiver to silence every sound on that channel as quickly as possible, without waiting for release stages.
example: B0 78 00 silences channel 1 immediately.

definition: Channel Mode message CC 121: returns a channel's controllers to their defaults, including putting pitch bend back to centre.
example: B0 79 00 resets the controllers on channel 1.

definition: Channel Mode message CC 122: connects or disconnects an instrument's own keyboard from its own sound engine, so the keyboard can drive a computer without playing the internal sounds twice.

A MIDI message containing manufacturer-defined or standard Universal SysEx data. In the MIDI 1.0 byte stream it begins with F0, has seven-bit ID/data bytes, and normally ends with F7; another status outside the real-time class also terminates it, while real-time messages can interleave.
example: F0 7D 01 02 F7 is a short SysEx message using the non-commercial ID 7D.

definition: The byte (or three bytes beginning 00) after F0 in a SysEx message that says whose format the data is in. IDs are assigned by the MIDI Association; 7D is for non-commercial use and 7E/7F are Universal.
example: A private DIY experiment can use ID 7D.

definition: End of Exclusive: the status byte F7 that ends a System Exclusive message.
example: F0 7D 01 F7: the final F7 is the EOX.

definition: System Exclusive messages with ID 7E (non-real-time) or 7F (real-time), whose formats are defined by the MIDI specifications themselves rather than by one manufacturer.
example: Device inquiry messages are Universal SysEx with ID 7E.

definition: MIDI system messages F1–F7 (F4 and F5 undefined), such as Song Position Pointer (F2) and Tune Request (F6). They apply to the whole system, not one channel, and they cancel running status.
example: F2 00 00 sets the song position to the start.

definition: A one-byte MIDI system message, F8 to FF, used for timing and transport: Timing Clock (F8), Start (FA), Continue (FB), Stop (FC), Active Sensing (FE) and System Reset (FF); F9 and FD are undefined. It may be sent at any time, even between the bytes of another message, and it does not cancel running status.
example: A receiver that sees 90 3C F8 64 handles the clock byte F8 and still reads 90 3C 64 as one Note On.

definition: The System Real-Time Timing Clock message, hexadecimal F8, sent twenty-four times per quarter note when synchronisation is needed. Clocks may continue while transport is stopped so a receiver can track tempo.
example: At 120 BPM, F8 arrives about every 20.8 ms.

definition: Pulses per quarter note: how many clock ticks make one beat. MIDI clock is fixed at 24 PPQN.
example: At 24 PPQN, six clocks make one sixteenth note.

definition: Beats per minute: the tempo of music, normally counting quarter notes.
example: At 120 BPM each beat lasts 0.5 s.

definition: A note lasting one beat in common 4/4 time; there are four in a 4/4 bar. Also called a crotchet.
example: At 60 BPM a quarter note lasts one second.

definition: A note lasting one quarter of a quarter note, also called a semiquaver. Sixteen fit in a 4/4 bar, and one corresponds to six MIDI Timing Clocks; the musical beat need not be a quarter note in every metre.
example: With MIDI clock, one sixteenth note is six F8 clocks.

definition: The System Real-Time messages Start (FA, play from the beginning), Continue (FB, resume from the current position) and Stop (FC), which control playback of synced sequencers.
example: Pressing play on the Digitakt with TRANSPORT SEND on sends FA.

definition: The System Common message F2 with a 14-bit value that tells a synced device where to continue from, counted in sixteenth notes (six MIDI clocks each).
example: F2 10 00 means 16 sixteenth notes (one 4/4 bar) from the start.

definition: The optional MIDI real-time message FE enables a receive-activity timeout. If no MIDI activity arrives for the specified approximately 300 ms interval after activation, the receiver silences its notes and returns to operation without Active Sensing; this protects against a lost connection.
The real-time byte FF, which asks receivers to return to their power-up state. It should be used sparingly, not sent automatically at power-up.
The 2020 extension of MIDI that adds higher-resolution values, per-note control and two-way capability discovery while keeping MIDI 1.0 compatibility. It carries messages in Universal MIDI Packets.
example: MIDI 2.0 velocity is 16-bit (65,536 steps) instead of 7-bit (128 steps).

definition: Universal MIDI Packet: MIDI 2.0's data format, which replaces the MIDI 1.0 byte stream with 32-, 64-, 96- or 128-bit packets organised as 16 groups of 16 channels. It can carry MIDI 1.0 and MIDI 2.0 messages.
MIDI Capability Inquiry: the part of MIDI 2.0 that lets two connected devices ask each other what they support, and on which Profiles and Property Exchange are built.
A MIDI-CI feature that lets devices get and set information such as patch lists and parameter names, using JSON-formatted data.

Optional UMP timing messages that let a sender describe event timing so a receiver can schedule playback with less transport-induced timing variation. Support and buffering determine the result; timestamps do not eliminate every source of delay.

A diagnostic tool displaying received MIDI messages or bytes, often decoded into channels, notes and controllers. Its output is evidence about the monitored point, not proof that every later stage received or rendered the events.
example: A MIDI monitor showing 92 40 5A proves the sequencer sent a note on channel 3.

definition: A MIDI method of sending absolute time positions (hours, minutes, seconds, frames) for synchronising to film or tape. It carries position but no tempo.
How long one bit lasts on a serial line: one divided by the bit rate.
example: At 31,250 bit/s a bit time is 32 µs, so a 10-bit MIDI byte takes 320 µs.

definition: An optional MIDI socket that re-sends a copy of everything arriving at MIDI IN, so several devices can be chained from one source.
example: Keyboard OUT to synth A IN, synth A THRU to synth B IN lets one keyboard play both.

definition: A connection pattern where devices are linked one after another, each passing the signal on to the next.
example: Three synths daisy-chained by MIDI THRU all receive the same notes.

definition: An older clock system (Sync24 or Sync48) that sends simple timing pulses over a DIN cable instead of MIDI messages. A Digitakt port set to DIN sync sends pulses, not MIDI data.
A transistor switched by light instead of by an electrical input. In an optocoupler it turns on when the internal LED lights.
The terminal of a diode or LED that current flows into when it conducts (the positive side).
The terminal of a diode or LED that current flows out of when it conducts (the negative side, usually marked with a band or flat edge).

A semiconductor component that conducts easily in its forward direction but blocks current in reverse, apart from a tiny leakage current, until the reverse voltage exceeds its breakdown rating. In a MIDI input, a diode wired the opposite way across the optocoupler's LED conducts if the loop is reversed, holding the LED's reverse voltage to about one diode forward drop so the LED is not damaged.
example: A 1N4148 small-signal diode (electrically equivalent to the 1N914 named in the MIDI electrical specification) drops at most 1 V forward at 10 mA, leaks at most 25 nA at 20 V reverse at 25 °C (far more when hot), and breaks down at 100 V or more.

definition: A small-signal switching diode named as D1 in the CA-033 reference MIDI input. It is connected antiparallel to the optocoupler LED to limit reverse voltage; confirm the actual diode’s ratings and wiring.
A Sharp high-speed optocoupler with a logic output, named in the MIDI electrical specification as suitable for MIDI inputs, with a recommended 280 Ω pull-up at 5 V.

An optocoupler named as acceptable in the MIDI electrical specification. Use the actual manufacturer’s datasheet to check supply, pull-up, timing and current requirements; its part number alone does not establish compatibility with a 3.3 V receiver.

An output that can only pull a line down to ground (through a transistor) and leaves it floating otherwise, so it needs a pull-up resistor to produce a high level. The voltage of the high level is set by where the pull-up connects.

A magnetic component whose impedance is deliberately high over a selected interference-frequency range. It can reduce RF currents but is not an ideal blocker, and its rated current and frequency behaviour must match the circuit.
How long a signal takes to switch from low to high (rise) or high to low (fall). MIDI asks for under 2 µs, much shorter than its 32 µs bit.
An unintended very-low-resistance connection, for example a signal wire touching ground, which can make far more current flow than a circuit is designed for.

A conductive screen around signal wires that helps control interference. In standard DIN MIDI the cable screen connects to pin 2 at both plugs, and MIDI IN has no DC ground path; optional RF capacitive connections are allowed by CA-033.
Tip-ring-sleeve: a jack plug with three contacts. The same plug can carry balanced mono audio, unbalanced stereo (headphones) or, on small devices, MIDI, so the device's documentation says which.

MIDI carried on a small TRS jack plus an adapter to 5-pin DIN. The standard (RP-054, 2018) is Type A: tip to DIN pin 5, ring to pin 4, sleeve to pin 2. Type B swaps tip and ring, so the wrong adapter passes no data.

The MIDI recommended practice approved in 2018 defining TRS MIDI pin wiring and cable requirements. It recommends 2.5 mm connectors but applies the same wiring rules to other sizes; Type A maps tip to DIN pin 5, ring to pin 4 and sleeve to pin 2.
A squarish USB connector used on the device side of a cable, for example on printers, audio interfaces and the Digitakt.
The later USB class specification that carries MIDI 2.0 Universal MIDI Packets natively and can fall back to USB MIDI 1.0.

USB standards for devices carrying audio-related functionality. The USB MIDI 1.0 specification defines MIDI Streaming as an Audio-class subclass, while audio sample streaming uses other interfaces; driver support depends on the host and class version.

Software implementing a standard device class such as USB MIDI. Systems that provide a compatible class driver can communicate with conforming devices without a device-specific vendor driver; availability and supported class versions depend on the operating system.
The USB Implementers Forum: the industry group that publishes the USB specifications, including the class definition for MIDI devices.

The four-byte USB MIDI 1.0 event format: a header containing Cable Number and Code Index Number, followed by up to three MIDI bytes and zero padding where needed. SysEx can span multiple packets, so not every packet is one complete MIDI message.
example: 09 90 3C 64 is a Note On on cable 0.

definition: The 4-bit number in a USB-MIDI packet header that picks one of up to 16 virtual MIDI cables (ports) sharing the same USB endpoint.
The 4-bit code in a USB-MIDI packet header that says what kind of message the packet holds and how many of its three MIDI bytes are used. For channel messages it equals the status byte's top nibble.
example: CIN 0x9 marks a Note On; CIN 0xB a Control Change.

definition: The USB generation with a 480 Mbit/s Hi-Speed mode, enough for multichannel audio as well as MIDI.

The USB signalling mode at 12 Mbit/s, introduced with USB 1.0 and kept in later versions. Many MIDI devices and microcontroller USB ports use it; even this mode gives far more raw bandwidth than 31,250 bit/s DIN MIDI, although real throughput depends on the host's scheduling and the device.
example: A class-compliant USB MIDI keyboard often connects at full speed (12 Mbit/s), while Hi-Speed USB 2.0 runs at 480 Mbit/s.

definition: A device that transfers USB data across an electrical isolation barrier. Breaking the ground path also requires an appropriate isolated power arrangement; check speed, device class, current and power limits rather than assuming every isolator supports an audio device.
PJRC's library for the Teensy 3.6 and 4.x USB host port, which lets a Teensy act as host to USB MIDI devices.
A connection in which both sides are equals and either may start a conversation. USB is not peer-to-peer: the host is always in charge.

Arrival at a receive buffer that has no free storage. Depending on the implementation, new or older data is discarded or an error is raised; a bounded MIDI receiver should count loss and recover without blocking the audio work.
example: A lost note-off byte from an overflow becomes a stuck note.

definition: A design in which a program is always in one of a small set of states and each input moves it to a next state according to fixed rules. A MIDI parser is a small state machine.
Able to play only one note at a time. A monophonic synth has one voice, so when several keys are held a note-priority rule decides which sounds.
How a polyphonic synth decides which of its voices plays each new note, and which note to cut (steal) when all voices are busy.
The rule a monophonic synth uses to pick which held key sounds: the most recently pressed (last-note), the lowest (low-note) or the highest (high-note).
example: Holding 60 then pressing 64: last-note and high-note play 64, low-note stays on 60.

definition: The list of keys currently held, in the order they were pressed, which a mono synth keeps so it can fall back to an earlier key when the sounding one is released.

A deliberately provided recovery control for stuck or unwanted notes. Define whether it cuts sound immediately or releases envelopes, and make it clear held and sustain-deferred note state and any chosen controller state.
Restarting a synth's envelopes from the beginning when a new note starts, even if a previous key is still held.

Smoothly connected notes. A typical monophonic synth legato mode changes pitch between overlapping held keys without restarting the envelope; exact retrigger and glide behaviour is an instrument design choice.
An on/off signal that is on while a note is held. When it closes, the envelopes move into their release stage.
The last part of a synth envelope, after the gate closes, during which the sound fades out over the release time.
A feature that plays the notes of a held chord one after another in a pattern, usually in time with a tempo clock.
A table listing which Control Change number controls which synth parameter, with each parameter's range and curve. It is needed to set up the controllers that will drive the synth.
A device or program that stores and plays back musical events (notes, controller changes) in time. The Digitakt has a step sequencer that can play external synths over MIDI.

A collection of synthesis settings making a sound; many instruments store and recall patches as presets or programs. Whether Program Change recalls one, and the associated bank numbering, depends on the receiving instrument.
A loudspeaker with no built-in amplifier, which must be driven from a power amplifier's speaker output.
The transducer on an electric guitar that turns string vibration into a small electrical signal at instrument level.
Connecting a low output impedance to a much higher input impedance (typically ten times or more) so that almost all the voltage is transferred. It is how audio line connections are designed.
example: 440 Ω into 10 kΩ loses only about 0.4 dB.

definition: Choosing a load and source impedance for a transfer objective. For a resistive source, an equal resistive load maximises delivered power and receives half the open-circuit voltage; with reactive impedances the maximum-power condition instead uses complex-conjugate matching. Audio line inputs usually use voltage bridging.

An audio connection where each signal is referenced to a shared return conductor, commonly also the shield. Ground-voltage differences or interference on that reference can enter the received signal; a stereo headphone cable carries two such signal channels with a shared return.

An audio interconnection whose signal conductors have matched impedances to the reference environment and feed a differential receiver. Interference can then appear predominantly as common mode and be rejected; rejection is finite and depends on the complete interconnection.
example: A 1/4-inch TRS cable from the Digitakt's impedance-balanced outputs into an interface's balanced line input rejects hum picked up along the cable.

definition: A balanced output arrangement that sends signal on one conductor and provides a matched impedance on the other. It can provide common-mode rejection into a suitable balanced receiver without requiring equal and opposite signal voltages.
example: Elektron describes the Digitakt's main outputs as impedance balanced.

definition: The two signal conductors of a balanced connection: on a TRS plug hot is the tip and cold is the ring; on XLR, normally pins 2 and 3.

An input that responds primarily to the voltage difference between two conductors. Rejection of the voltage common to both is finite and limited by the circuit’s common-mode range and rejection ratio.

The reactive part of impedance, caused by energy storage in capacitance or inductance. For an ideal capacitor its magnitude decreases as frequency rises; the numerical examples here use that magnitude rather than the signed complex impedance.
example: A 0.1 µF capacitor is about 26.5 kΩ at 60 Hz but only about 0.16 Ω at 10 MHz.

definition: A capacitor construction offering substantial capacitance in a compact package. Common aluminium electrolytics are polarised and have voltage, ripple-current, temperature and lifetime limits; bipolar versions also exist, so check the actual part.
How much a capacitor's value changes with the voltage across it. Some ceramic types change a lot, which can distort audio; film capacitors change very little.
Centring a signal halfway between a single supply's 0 V and its positive rail so it can swing both ways.
example: On a 3.3 V supply, mid-scale is 1.65 V.

definition: Operating a circuit from a positive supply and a zero-volt reference rather than separate positive and negative rails. Many analogue stages then use a DC bias for bipolar audio, while other architectures such as a charge-pump output can produce ground-centred signals.
An output stage designed to send line-level audio down a cable into the next device's input.
The steady DC voltages and currents a circuit sits at with no signal. Pushing DC into an input shifts it and reduces headroom.
A circuit that uses capacitors switched at high speed to make a different supply voltage, such as a negative rail from a positive one.
An interface input socket that accepts either an XLR plug (mic path) or a 1/4-inch jack (line or instrument path).
A hand-held meter that measures voltage, current and resistance; on DC voltage it shows a signal's DC offset.
A display showing a signal's level, used to keep peaks below clipping.
The frequency of the AC mains supply: 50 Hz in the UK and Europe, 60 Hz in North America.

Protective earth connects exposed conductive parts of appropriate equipment to a protective conductor, helping fault protection disconnect the supply. It must never be disconnected to treat audio hum; signal-reference ground and protective earth serve different roles.

Radio frequency: electrical variations associated with radio signals and interference. The MIDI examples here concern megahertz-frequency interference, where shielding and real component behaviour matter; radio frequency is not simply a synonym for all frequencies above hearing.

Routing an input to monitoring outputs inside an audio interface while bypassing the computer’s audio processing and buffers. The remaining delay depends on the interface’s analogue or digital monitoring design.

The number of audio samples processed or transferred in a chunk. Dividing by sample rate gives the chunk duration and helps establish processing budgets; the actual latency depends on the buffering, driver and hardware architecture.
example: A 128-sample buffer at 48 kHz holds about 2.7 ms of audio; 256 samples holds about 5.3 ms.

definition: Passing a track’s incoming signal to its output for listening. Live’s In setting monitors continuously; Auto monitors an armed track except while it plays clips; Off disables that software monitoring and can be used with an interface’s direct monitoring.
A track in a DAW that records and plays audio (as opposed to MIDI).
Enabling a DAW track to record from its input; an armed track records when you press record.
Ableton Live's input selector on a track: chooses where the track's audio comes from, such as Ext. In and an interface channel.
An Ableton Live device that sends MIDI to external hardware and brings its audio back from chosen interface inputs, with a Hardware Latency setting to correct timing.
The External Instrument setting in Ableton Live for delays through external gear that Live cannot detect, entered in milliseconds or samples.
example: A 3 ms delay at 48 kHz is 144 samples.

definition: Ableton Live's automatic correction for the processing delays of devices so tracks stay aligned; the Hardware Latency slider depends on it.
The selected source of tempo clock in a synchronised setup. Receivers follow it; choose a defined direction so devices do not send competing clocks back to one another.
example: With the Digitakt as clock master, Live follows it via EXT sync.

definition: The Swedish company that makes the Digitakt and other instruments.
Elektron's software that streams audio and parameter control between its instruments and a computer over USB.
A track whose recorded or sequenced material is MIDI events. A Digitakt MIDI track controls an external instrument; in a DAW, a software instrument on a MIDI track can turn those events into audio.
On the Digitakt II, the machine you assign to a track to turn it into a MIDI track.
Elektron's term for a step that is switched on in the sequencer; on a MIDI track each trig sends a note (or up to four for a chord).
An Elektron sequencer feature that gives one step its own value for a parameter, such as a different CC value on just that trig.
On a Digitakt MIDI track, the source page where CHAN, bank, program and pitch bend, aftertouch, mod wheel and breath sends are set.
The Digitakt MIDI-track setting on the SRC page that chooses the MIDI channel (OFF or 1–16) the track sends on.
The Digitakt trig setting for note length, which decides when the note off is sent. The original Digitakt manual lists an INF (infinite) value that holds the note indefinitely.
The Digitakt MIDI setting (in MIDI CONFIG > PORT CONFIG) that makes the MIDI OUT socket send MIDI, or DIN 24/48 sync pulses instead.
Digitakt sync settings (MIDI CONFIG > SYNC) that choose whether it sends or follows MIDI clock and Start/Stop transport messages.
The Digitakt setting that chooses what its USB port does: Overbridge, USB MIDI, or USB audio and MIDI.
A DC power plug whose inner (centre) contact is positive and outer sleeve negative. Using a supply of the wrong polarity can damage a device.
A circuit diagram showing components as symbols and the connections between them.
Do it yourself: built by you rather than bought ready-made.
Whether a connector has pins (male, usually the plug) or holes (female, usually the socket). MIDI devices have female DIN sockets and cables are male-to-male.
MIDI uses three pins of the 5-pin DIN connector: pin 4 is the current source, pin 5 the current sink (data line) and pin 2 the shield, grounded at the transmitter only. Pins 1 and 3 are unconnected.

Naming a note with its letter plus an octave number. The numbering differs between products: middle C (MIDI note 60) is C4 in scientific pitch notation, C3 in Ableton Live and C5 in the original Digitakt manual.
The switch in Ableton Live's control bar that makes Live follow tempo from an external MIDI clock source.
The Digitakt trig setting for note velocity sent on a MIDI track.
Digitakt MIDI-track settings that add up to three extra notes to each trig, turning it into a chord.

A Digitakt menu for transferring supported project, pattern and sound/preset data through SysEx. The available categories and procedures depend on whether the unit is an original Digitakt or Digitakt II and on its firmware.

A MIDI channel mode for monophonic voice allocation. With Omni off, separate received MIDI channels can control separate monophonic voices; with Omni on, received channels control one monophonic voice. It does not specify the number of audio output channels.

A MIDI channel mode assigning simultaneous note messages to multiple voices up to the receiver’s capacity, on the channels selected by Omni and Basic Channel settings. It describes note allocation rather than mono or stereo audio outputs.
The coarse and fine seven-bit quantities used to assemble some MIDI 1.0 fourteen-bit values. Although often called MSB and LSB in MIDI, each part contributes seven value bits rather than eight.

The time occupied by one complete MIDI UART frame, including start and stop bits. At the nominal 31,250-bit-per-second rate this is 320 microseconds, so line time counts ten bits for each eight-bit byte.
An integer operation that moves bits towards the lower-value positions. For the non-negative MIDI integers here, shifting right by seven discards the low seven bits and keeps the coarse part.
An integer operation that moves bits towards higher-value positions and fills the low positions with zeros. The MIDI examples use sufficiently wide non-negative integers so no required bits are lost.

The connected path followed by the sound waveform, from the synthesiser output through an interface or mixer to monitoring or recording. It is distinct from the MIDI messages instructing a synth what to play.

The analogue electrical signal from an unbuffered instrument pickup, such as a guitar pickup. Its voltage and frequency-dependent source impedance vary with the instrument and playing, so it needs an appropriately high-impedance input.

The elapsed time from an audio input change to hearing the corresponding output through the selected monitoring path. Software monitoring includes driver, buffering, processing and converter delays; direct monitoring bypasses the computer path.

An audio line with signal-conductor impedances matched to the reference environment, feeding a differential input. Equal interference is rejected according to the receiver’s finite common-mode rejection; a shield helps but is not the defining feature of balance.
Device-specific software supplied for a manufacturer’s hardware, in contrast with a driver implementing a standard USB device class. Whether one is needed depends on the supported class and features.

A device configured to use an external tempo source rather than generate the governing clock itself. Live can follow MIDI Clock from the selected input; this role differs from a computer’s USB host role.

Resistance or other protective circuitry in a DIN MIDI output that limits loop and fault current. CA-033 requires current limiting on both output pins; the circuit must also respect resistor power and driver current ratings.
The Digitakt settings menu for MIDI synchronisation, ports and channel configuration. Use the exact model/OS manual because the available options and labels can change.
The Digitakt MIDI settings section controlling port functions and output routes. In particular a port configured for DIN synchronisation pulses does not send MIDI note data.
The port configuration setting selecting where MIDI output is sent, such as the DIN MIDI port, USB, or both. This is separate from choosing a track’s MIDI channel.

MIDI source-page controls: PB sends pitch bend, AT aftertouch, MW the modulation wheel controller and BC the breath controller. The receiving synth decides how the supported messages affect its sound.
The Digitakt filter-button parameter page. On MIDI tracks it provides CC controls rather than an audio filter: the exact layout and number of pages depend on the model.
The Digitakt amplitude-button parameter page. On MIDI tracks it provides assignable CC controls rather than processing audio; consult the model’s MIDI machine/track pages.

MIDI track controls for bank selection and program change. BANK and SBNK supply bank-related control values and PROG selects the program; the receiving instrument must support the chosen numbering and bank convention.
A modifier key on the Digitakt used with other keys to select alternate functions. For example the Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual uses FUNC with SRC to open the machine menu.
The Digitakt track-selection key used with a numbered trig key to select a track. Original Digitakt MIDI tracks occupy nine through sixteen; Digitakt II tracks can be assigned a MIDI machine.

The stated RMS voltage used as the zero point for a logarithmic audio level. The dBu reference is approximately 0.7746 V RMS and the dBV reference is 1 V RMS; compare levels using the same reference rather than subtracting unlike scales.
example: A signal of 1 V RMS is 0 dBV, or approximately +2.2 dBu.
